This is basically about the failings of an economic system based on debt. Every Eurozone country is inextricably linked to one another by debt - imagine it a little like using a Mastercard (Greece) to pay for your mortgage (Euro), then a Visa (Portugal) to pay for your Mastercard and then an American Express (Spain) to pay for the Visa card, and on and on.

If Greece decides to go bankrupt then they will default on paying their debt to the other EU nations who rely on this payment as they also have debt to pay for their national borrowing.

This then affects the derivatives markets and when investors start cashing in, everyone will see that most of the debt is based on nothing solid in the material world, the Euro will devalue, and the feared runs on the banks will be seen.

It will be like the proverbial domino effect.

Greece isn't being given the money for free, basically, and doesn't like the terms. This is another stunt in a long line of the current Greek government's attempts to negotiate a better deal.

As for watching Greece burn, it's pretty much the Eurogroup that's doing the burning, since the terms of the bailout are largely policy dictates. They might think they're helping, but it's far more likely that Greece is being made an example of for the rest of Europe's spendthrifts as a way to preserve the Euro.
